name: Cobalt
poem: A clean, medium-deep blue invented by alchemists chasing real ultramarine — a colour that made blue-and-white porcelain possible and now powers the batteries in every phone.

recipe.note: A clean medium blue, calm and slightly cool.

lenses.label: Art History
lenses.intro: Cobalt blue made one of the most globally recognisable art forms possible — and then, in oil paint, became the favourite blue of the Impressionists.

entries.title: Ming Blue and White
entries.blurb: The exact cobalt blue of Ming porcelain depended on imported Persian "Mohammedan blue" cobalt ore — refined into the colour that defines Chinese export ceramics.

entries.title: Delftware
entries.blurb: Delft potters imitated Chinese blue and white using local cobalt — and built a colour that is now indistinguishable from "Delft" in any colour theory book.

entries.title: Monet's Water Lilies
entries.blurb: The water in Monet's late lily ponds is built on cobalt blue — a pigment Monet specifically requested over ultramarine for its slightly cooler edge and its slow drying time.

lenses.label: Fashion
lenses.intro: Cobalt is the blue brands reach for when they want intensity without the historical weight of ultramarine or the everydayness of navy.

entries.title: Royal Blue Evening Wear
entries.blurb: "Royal blue" is essentially saturated cobalt — a colour designers reach for whenever they need a dress to look photographed rather than worn.

entries.title: Cobalt Glass Jewellery
entries.blurb: Bohemian glassmakers refined cobalt-blue glass into beads, vases, and costume jewellery — affordable colour that mimicked sapphire well enough to pass at distance.

entries.title: Blue Period Workwear
entries.blurb: From American police uniforms to flight-attendant suits, mid-tone cobalt has become the default colour of professional trust — neither command-black nor casual navy.

lenses.label: Nature
lenses.intro: Cobalt is one of those metals that gives folklore as much as chemistry — and the modern world's quiet dependence on it is a story still being written.

entries.title: Cobalt Ore
entries.blurb: Pinkish-grey ore historically considered worthless — German miners blamed the unhelpful rock on "kobolds," mischievous mountain spirits. The element kept the name.

entries.title: Blue Glass Beach
entries.blurb: Sea-tumbled fragments of cobalt-blue glass wash up wherever boats have sunk for two centuries — beach-glass collectors prize them above all other colours.

entries.title: Cobalt-Blue Tarantula
entries.blurb: A spider from Myanmar whose legs are an unmistakable cobalt — the colour comes from microscopic structures on the hairs, not pigment. One of nature's few true blues.

lenses.label: Pop Culture
lenses.intro: Cobalt has become one of the most strategically important metals on Earth — every electric vehicle and laptop battery depends on it.

entries.title: Lithium-Ion Batteries
entries.blurb: Every iPhone, electric car, and laptop battery contains cobalt — and roughly 70% of the world's supply comes from artisanal mines in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

entries.title: Iron Man's Reactor
entries.blurb: The fictional "arc reactor" glows the exact saturated cobalt-blue of every "clean energy" trope — a colour Hollywood reaches for when an audience needs to read "future."

entries.title: Cobalt-60
entries.blurb: The radioactive isotope cobalt-60 was the first widely used source for cancer radiotherapy — and gave the element a second 20th-century reputation as a destroyer of cells.

lenses.label: Etymology
lenses.intro: Cobalt is the rare element whose name is a slur — a curse the miners hurled at the ore before anyone knew what was inside it.

entries.title: "Kobold"
entries.blurb: Saxon silver-miners blamed Crystal-blue "useless" ore on goblins who supposedly switched the silver for poison vapour. The word "cobalt" preserved the curse.

entries.title: Element 27
entries.blurb: Brandt isolated cobalt from "useless" Saxon ore — the first metal discovered in the modern scientific sense. He published partly to vindicate the miners' suspicion that something was there.

entries.title: "Mohammedan Blue"
entries.blurb: The Persian-source cobalt that gave Ming porcelain its colour was called "hui hui qing" in Chinese — "Mohammedan blue," a name preserving its Islamic-world origin.

lenses.label: Symbolism
lenses.intro: Cobalt's symbolism has shifted constantly — from goblin curse to imperial export to clean-energy salvation — but always carries an edge of value just beyond reach.

entries.title: German Folklore
entries.blurb: The kobolds of German mining folklore weren't entirely malevolent — they sometimes helped honest miners. Cobalt-the-element kept the mountain-spirit's reputation.

entries.title: Imperial China
entries.blurb: Cobalt-blue porcelain was the largest export of imperial China — paid for in silver, shipped across the Pacific, used as currency in colonial trade. A colour as money.

entries.title: Conflict Mineral
entries.blurb: Today cobalt is on the EU's list of critical raw materials and a focus of conflict-mineral reporting — the colour of every smartphone, sourced under conditions buyers prefer not to see.
